title: Optimal noisy sequential multiparameter quantum sensing
authors: Andrew Tanggara, Lorcán O Conlon, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Kishor Bharti
abstract: The most general strategy for estimating parameters of a quantum channel is to probe the channel many times sequentially with the help of coherent ancillary systems. However, finding the strategy that minimizes the mean-squared error (MSE) is a notoriously hard problem, requiring optimization over the initial probe state, intermediate evolutions, final measurement, and classical postprocessing. In this work, we study how the minimum attainable MSE can be bounded from below in this setting. We propose a lower bound for the MSE of any physically implementable sequential sensing strategy that applies to estimating parameters of any physical quantum evolution, including quantum channels probed over multiple time steps under temporally correlated noise and general temporally correlated quantum processes. We show that this lower bound can be formulated as a semidefinite program (SDP). Our bound generalizes the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound (that applies to parameter estimation tasks with separable measurements) to the regime where the quantum channel can be accessed sequentially multiple times. For regular finite-dimensional single-parameter sequential estimation tasks admitting an optimal strategy, we show that our SDP bound is tight and provide a procedure to obtain a locally optimal strategy from the SDP optimizer. Using our optimization bound, we compute the MSE lower bound and derive new protocols for several other physically motivated problems including error-corrected quantum sensing under an unknown correlated noise model, multiparameter estimation, and estimation with qudit systems.
summary: This paper develops a powerful Semidefinite Programming (SDP) framework to establish lower bounds on the Mean-Squared Error (MSE) for estimating parameters of quantum channels through sequential probing. It generalizes existing quantum estimation bounds to account for multiple time steps and correlated noise. The results provide new, rigorous benchmarks for designing optimal quantum sensing protocols in various physical systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the notoriously difficult problem of finding the optimal strategy to estimate parameters of a quantum channel when the channel is probed multiple times sequentially.
main_result: The authors propose a general lower bound for the Mean-Squared Error (MSE) of any physically implementable sequential sensing strategy, formulated as a Semidefinite Program (SDP). This bound is shown to be tight for single-parameter tasks.
method: The core method involves deriving an SDP-based lower bound that generalizes the Nagaoka-Hayashi bound to the regime of sequential measurements, utilizing concepts like the quantum comb formalism.
model_or_system: The model involves estimating parameters $	heta$ of a quantum channel $\Lambda_	heta$ by sequentially probing the channel multiple times ($T$ steps) using coherent ancillary systems and performing final measurements.
key_observables: Mean-Squared Error ($	ext{MSE}_	heta$), Quantum Fisher Information ($	ext{QFI}$), and the covariance matrix of the parameter estimates.
important_parameters: Number of time steps ($T$), number of parameters ($m$), and the specific noise model (e.g., correlated Pauli noise).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of an optimal strategy and provides local attainability results for the SDP bound in single-parameter cases.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the MSE lower bound for sequential estimation tasks (e.g., Pauli-Z or X/Y rotations) under various noise levels, comparing the bound to the expected Heisenberg scaling ($1/T^2$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general SDP lower bound for sequential sensing, then applying it to specific physical scenarios like single-parameter estimation (e.g., Pauli rotations) under both independent and correlated noise models, and finally comparing multi-step vs. single-step protocols.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous, computationally tractable bounds (via SDP) on the ultimate precision limits for quantum metrology in complex, realistic settings involving sequential measurements and correlated noise, which is crucial for designing practical quantum sensors.
